# SK4022 — The struct is never mutated and is not `readonly`

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A struct with only readonly state and no member that assigns `this` can be `readonly`, which deletes the defensive copies.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Performance |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | 7.2 |
| Since | 1.3 |

## Why

The compiler cannot know that a struct's members leave it alone, so wherever the struct is reached through storage it may not write — a `readonly` field, an `in` parameter, a `ref readonly` return, a `foreach` variable — it copies the whole value before every member call. `SK2005` and `SK4007` report two consequences of exactly that. The `readonly` modifier is the declaration that removes the doubt: the compiler verifies that no member writes to the instance and then stops emitting the copies. The keyword is not a hint or a tuning parameter; it is a fact about the type that the type already satisfied and had not written down.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
struct Point {
    public readonly int X;
    public readonly int Y;

    public int Length => X + Y;
}
```

Write:

```csharp
readonly struct Point {
    public readonly int X;
    public readonly int Y;

    public int Length => X + Y;
}
```

## When it does not fire

The proof is the compiler's own rule for `readonly struct`, checked before the keyword is proposed: every instance field must already be `readonly`, no instance property or indexer may have a `set` accessor, and no member may assign to `this`, pass it by `ref` or `out`, or increment it. ⚠ **A captured primary-constructor parameter is a field the struct never declares**, and a struct that writes one is declined: `readonly` makes the capture readonly too, and the write becomes CS9114, CS9116 or CS9117. Found by applying every safe fix to every fixture; the shape sat in an `SK2194` positive. ⚠ What counts as a write is shared with `SK2194` (#408), so the two cannot disagree again: assignment of every kind including deconstruction, `++`/`--`, `ref`/`out`, a writable `ref` local, and a write to a member or indexer of a capture whose type is not a reference type. A write to a member of a class-typed capture leaves the capture alone and does not decline. ⚠ A member write through an unconstrained type parameter compiles under `readonly` — against a defensive copy — and is declined anyway, because when the argument is a struct the fix would silently redirect the write to a copy. A parameter that is only read stays eligible, and so does one written only in a variable initializer or an `init` accessor, the compiler's own two exceptions. `init` accessors are admitted, because a `readonly struct` permits them. Excluded outright: a struct already `readonly`, a `partial` or multiply-declared struct, a `ref struct`, a `record struct` — where the modifier would turn positional `set` accessors into `init` and change the public API — anything `unsafe` or holding a `fixed` buffer or a pointer, a field-like `event`, whose backing field cannot be readonly, and a struct that already spells `readonly` on one of its members. Nested types inside the struct are not searched, because `this` there is a different instance. ⚠ **The modifier is not a no-op for consumers even though it is source-compatible**: an `in` parameter and a `readonly` field stop copying, so a member that returned a value derived from a stale copy now returns the current one. That is the bug the copies were hiding rather than a behaviour the rule breaks, but it is a change and it is why the finding is a suggestion rather than a warning.
